764.title: Kyiv's baptism (988)
764.hook: Prince Vladimir's people are baptized in the Dnieper, a shared root of Orthodox and Eastern Catholics
764.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians and Ukrainian Greek Catholics both keep a feast of Saint Vladimir and remember the baptism of Kyiv; Catholics of the Latin rite join in praying for Ukraine and for unity among Christians.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charlemagne: a crown in Rome, and schools beside it. Your line was crowns and cathedrals.

A wide river runs past a city on high bluffs. On the bank stand priests in vestments, come from the Greek lands to the south. Into the water walk the people of Kyiv, the old chronicle says, some up to their necks, some to their chests, the young ones near the shore, parents holding their babies. The priests stand and say the prayers over them. A whole city, baptized together in the Dnieper. Today, Kyiv's baptism.
screen: `A RIVER BELOW THE BLUFFS.` → `PRIESTS ON THE BANK.` → `A CITY IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Our main source is the old chronicle of Kyiv, written by monks, sometimes called the Tale of Bygone Years. It tells the story of Vladimir, grand prince of Kyiv. His envoys, it says, came back from a liturgy in the great church of Constantinople and said they hadn't known whether they were in heaven or on earth, only that God dwells there among people. The beauty of the worship moved them. Vladimir himself was baptized, married a sister of the emperors in Constantinople, and came home with priests. Then he sent word through the city: anyone, rich or poor, who did not come to the river would be counted the prince's enemy. That was a command, not an invitation, and it's worth hearing honestly, the day after Charlemagne. The chronicle says the people came gladly. Whatever was in each heart, they came, and the chronicle tells the scene with real tenderness: people standing in the water, the priests praying, and Vladimir glad that he and his people knew God. This baptism is a shared root. Orthodox churches of Ukraine, Russia and Belarus trace their faith to that river, and so does the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church, which prays in the Eastern way and is in communion with Rome. Both remember Vladimir as a saint. One river, two families who each call it the beginning. The Gospels use the same Greek word, baptizo, when Jesus sends the apostles out to baptize all nations. A people's faith beginning not in a building, but in water, out under the sky.
screen: `HEAVEN OR EARTH?` · `VLADIMIR COMES HOME.` · `EVERYONE TO THE RIVER.` · `ONE ROOT, TWO FAMILIES.` · then, large: `BAPTIZED IN THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Let your breath move slowly, like water past a bank, and with each breath out, think of one person in Ukraine you will never meet: someone waking up there today, someone far from home. If you pray, ask God's peace and protection for everyone who lives there, in your own words or with an Our Father; if you don't, simply hold them in mind, one breath at a time.
Kyiv's baptism. Prince Vladimir's people baptized in the Dnieper, a root shared by Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians. Today's word.
Your line: baptized in the river. Water, prayers, and a whole city at the shore. Until tomorrow.

765.title: Two lungs
765.hook: John Paul II said the Church must breathe with both lungs, East and West
765.howItsDone: The Catholic Church includes both the Latin Church and Eastern Catholic Churches with their own liturgies, and Catholics pray for unity with the Orthodox, especially in the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kyiv's baptism, a whole city in the Dnieper. Your line was baptized in the river.

Take one slow breath, right now, and notice it. Both sides of your chest rise. You don't decide to use the left lung or the right one; they work together, or you work less well. A pope from Poland, John Paul the Second, reached for exactly this picture when he wrote about Christians of East and West, long apart, and the Church they belong to. Not a ladder, not a building, not an army. A pair of lungs. Today, two lungs.
screen: `ONE SLOW BREATH.` → `BOTH SIDES RISE.` → `A POPE'S PICTURE.`

segments.voice: Across this stretch, this path has met the first Christians and the Fathers, and they came from both halves of the old world: Greek speakers like John Chrysostom and John of Damascus, Latin speakers like Augustine, Leo and Gregory, monks in Egypt, on Athos and at Monte Cassino. For a long time they belonged to one Church, praying in different languages and styles. Then East and West drifted apart over language, politics and theology, and in the end broke communion with each other. That wound is still open. Catholics and Orthodox Christians share the sacraments and the apostles, but don't yet share one table. Pope John Paul the Second wrote, in his letter on Christian unity, that the Church must breathe with her two lungs, East and West. The Eastern traditions, their icons, their chant, their long liturgies, their monks, aren't decoration on a Latin Church. They are half of its breathing. And inside the Catholic Church itself, Eastern Catholic Churches, like the Ukrainian Greek Catholics you met yesterday, already pray in the Eastern way in communion with Rome. Underneath is an older picture still. In Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims, God "breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Breath is a gift before it's an achievement. And unity, for John Paul, was something to pray for, not to force. His letter takes its name from Jesus's prayer in John's Gospel: "That they all may be one."
screen: `FATHERS FROM BOTH HALVES.` · `A WOUND STILL OPEN.` · `BREATHE WITH TWO LUNGS.` · `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.` · then, large: `EAST AND WEST.`

segments.voice: Put one hand on each side of your chest, breathe in slowly, filling both sides, and let it go; then once more, deeper. Rest your hands and notice both sides working without being asked. If you pray, let the words from John, that they all may be one, ride the breath; if not, simply rest in breathing.
Two lungs. John Paul the Second's picture of the Church breathing with both its traditions, East and West. Today's word.

766.title: What the Fathers gave
766.hook: a way of reading scripture inside a praying Church
766.howItsDone: Catholics meet the Church Fathers in the Office of Readings, where a passage from scripture is followed by a passage from a Father, and in homilies and catechesis that quote them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two lungs: the Church breathing East and West. Your line was east and west.

Open a Bible alone at the kitchen table and it can feel like walking into a huge house by yourself: rooms everywhere, doors you don't know how to open. Now walk in again with people who lived there, who prayed in those rooms, argued over them, died rather than leave. Ignatius, Polycarp, Irenaeus. Athanasius and Basil. Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome. John Chrysostom. Leo, Benedict, Gregory. Today closes this first stretch of the year with one question: what did all of them leave behind? Today's word is Church Fathers.
screen: `A HUGE HOUSE, ALONE.` → `NOW WITH PEOPLE WHO LIVED THERE.` → `WHAT DID THEY LEAVE?`

segments.voice: The Church Fathers are the teachers of the early centuries whom the Church trusts as witnesses to its faith: bishops, monks, a few laymen, and alongside them women like Macrina and Paula, whom you've met too. What they left isn't mainly a set of answers. It's a way of reading. First, they read scripture as one story. The Old Testament and the New were one book about one God, and Christ was the key that opened it. Second, they read it inside the liturgy. Sermons like Leo's and Gregory's were preached at Mass, to people who had just heard the readings. Scripture wasn't a private hobby; it was the Church's own voice, read aloud, then broken open like bread. Third, they read it to love. Augustine wrote that anyone who thinks they've understood scripture, but whose reading doesn't build up love of God and neighbor, hasn't understood it yet. And Gregory the Great said that the words of scripture grow with the one who reads them. Come back older, and the same verse is bigger. Catholic teaching today says scripture is meant to be read within the living tradition of the whole Church, and the Fathers are a large part of what that means. The Psalms put it simply, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths." The Fathers carried that lamp a long time before handing it on.
screen: `ONE STORY, ONE KEY.` · `READ INSIDE THE LITURGY.` · `READ IT TO LOVE.` · `IT GROWS WITH THE READER.` · then, large: `READ IT WITH THE FATHERS.`

segments.voice: Let one name from this stretch come to mind, whichever surfaces first: Augustine's restless heart, Bede finishing, Leo walking out to meet Attila, Isidore, who said that when we read, God speaks. Rest with that person for a moment, as if they were sitting beside you at the kitchen table. If you pray, thank God for the people who handed the lamp on.
Church Fathers. The early teachers the Church trusts as witnesses to its faith, who left a way of reading scripture inside a praying Church. Today's word.
Your line: read it with the fathers. Tomorrow the story turns to the bishops meeting together. See you then.

767.title: What a council is
767.hook: bishops from across the whole Church gather, with the pope, to settle a question too big for one person
767.howItsDone: Catholics receive the teaching of the ecumenical councils as binding on the whole Church; the Nicene Creed said at Sunday Mass grew from the early councils.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the Church Fathers gave: a way of reading scripture inside a praying Church. Your line was read it with the fathers.

A hospital waiting room, late at night. A family has a hard question in front of it: how to care for a parent who can't live alone anymore. Everyone has a view. Someone talks too long; someone goes quiet. And at some point, if it goes well, they land on something they can all stand behind, and they say it out loud, together. The Church has done this too, on questions at the heart of its faith, with bishops in the room instead of brothers and sisters. A new stretch of the year starts today, with a word: ecumenical council.
screen: `A WAITING ROOM, LATE AT NIGHT.` → `EVERYONE HAS A VIEW.` → `ONE ANSWER, SAID TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: The pattern starts in the Bible. In the Acts of the Apostles, the first followers of Jesus hit a question that could have split them: when people who weren't Jewish came to believe, did they need to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses? The text says, "And the apostles and ancients assembled to consider of this matter." A long debate followed. Peter spoke. Paul and Barnabas told what they had seen God do. James proposed a way forward. And the letter they sent out carries a remarkable phrase: "For it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us." Not us alone. The Holy Ghost, and us. Some readers call that gathering in Jerusalem the first council. Later, when the Church had spread far beyond Jerusalem, it met the same way, only larger. An ecumenical council is a gathering of bishops from across the whole Church, together with the pope, to settle a question of faith or life for everyone. The Catechism says the college of bishops exercises its authority over the whole Church in a solemn way in such a council, and that no council is ecumenical unless Peter's successor confirms it, or at least accepts it as such. Catholics believe the Holy Spirit guards what the bishops, with the pope, teach together as definitive on faith and morals. Orthodox Christians honor the early councils too. Over the coming weeks, this path walks through several councils, each beginning with a question too big for one person.
screen: `A QUESTION IN ACTS.` · `THE APOSTLES ASSEMBLED.` · then, large: `IT HATH SEEMED GOOD TO THE HOLY GHOST AND TO US.` · then: `BISHOPS FROM EVERYWHERE, WITH THE POPE.` · `ONE QUESTION, ANSWERED TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time you decided something with others, a family, a team, a parish council, and look not at the outcome but at the room: who spoke, who listened, what it took to come to one mind. If it went badly, notice that too without replaying the argument, and ask what the group leaned on besides its own cleverness. If you pray, give thanks for the people at that table with you.

768.title: Nicaea, 325: the question
768.hook: bishops, some still scarred from persecution, gather to answer Arius
768.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the pope and their own bishop by name in the Eucharistic Prayer at every Mass, and the Creed said on Sundays grew from the Council of Nicaea.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ecumenical council: bishops from across the Church, with the pope, settling a question for everyone. Your line was they met together.

A priest in Alexandria named Arius is preaching a line that catches on; later writers say his ideas were even set to tunes people could sing. The line, in plain words: there was a time when the Son of God did not exist. The Father alone has no beginning. The Son came after, the first and greatest of all he made, but made. A creature. His bishop, Alexander, objects. The quarrel jumps from church to church, city to city, until no single bishop can settle it. Today, the city where the Church gathered to answer: Nicaea.
screen: `ARIUS, A PRIEST IN ALEXANDRIA.` → `THE SON WAS MADE.` → `TOO BIG FOR ONE BISHOP.`

segments.voice: Nicaea was a city in Asia Minor, in what is now Turkey. By the account of the historian Eusebius, the emperor Constantine called bishops there from across his empire. The Catechism names it the first ecumenical council, and gives its year as 325. Look at who walked in. The historian Theodoret describes some of them. One bishop, Paul, had lost the use of both hands; a red-hot iron had been put to them under persecution. Others had lost an eye, or been crippled. Theodoret says the gathering looked like an army of martyrs. Scarred bishops. Some of these men had paid in their own bodies for saying that Jesus is Lord, and the question in front of them was what, exactly, they meant by it. It's a question from the Gospels. Jesus asks his disciples, "But whom do you say that I am?" Arius had an answer: someone great, the highest of creatures, but a creature. The bishops listened, argued, and gave a different answer, the one this path opens tomorrow in a single word. They were not theorists in a comfortable room. When they asked who he is, they were asking about the one they had suffered for. Catholics believe the Holy Spirit guided that council, and the creed that grew from it is still said at Mass on Sundays.
screen: `A CITY CALLED NICAEA.` · `AN ARMY OF MARTYRS.` · then, large: `BUT WHOM DO YOU SAY THAT I AM?` · then: `ASKED BY PEOPLE WHO HAD SUFFERED.`

769.title: One in being
769.hook: the Son is of the same substance as the Father, the word said at Mass on Sundays
769.howItsDone: Catholics say the Nicene Creed together at Mass on Sundays and solemnities, and the Roman Missal asks all to bow at the words about the Son becoming man.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nicaea: bishops, some with burned hands and lost eyes, gathered to answer Arius. Your line was scarred bishops.

Sunday Mass, after the homily. The church stands and says the Creed together, and a few lines in comes a long, Latin-sounding word: consubstantial. It sounds like something from a chemistry class. Said in a breath, and the next line is already under way. That word is the answer the scarred bishops gave at Nicaea. Arius had said the Son was made. The council's reply is folded into this one clumsy, careful word.
screen: `SUNDAY, THE CREED.` → `A LONG, LATIN-SOUNDING WORD.` → `NICAEA'S ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The bishops answered Arius with a Greek word: homoousios, of the same substance, the same being. The Catechism says the council at Nicaea confessed the Son as begotten, not made, of the same substance as the Father. In Latin that became consubstantialis; in English, consubstantial, or in older words, of one substance. The old Book of Common Prayer gives the creed's lines like this: "God of God, Light of Light, Very God of very God, Begotten, not made, Being of one substance with the Father." The Catholic Mass in English says it now as God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God. Same claim. Why did the bishops care so much? If the Son is a creature, however grand, then in Jesus God sent someone else. If the Son is of one being with the Father, then in Jesus God came himself. John's Gospel opens on exactly that: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." And Jesus says in John, "I and the Father are one." Look at the creed's pictures. Light from light: a flame lit from a flame is not less fire than the first. Begotten, not made: a builder makes a house, something other than himself; a parent begets a child, someone of the same kind. Some readers notice the irony: a term from philosophy, chosen to guard what the bishops read in the Gospels. Clumsy on the tongue, and that is partly the point. It doesn't let the answer slide.
screen: `HOMOOUSIOS: OF THE SAME SUBSTANCE.` · `GOD SENT SOMEONE, OR CAME HIMSELF?` · `LIGHT FROM LIGHT.` · then, large: `BEGOTTEN, NOT MADE.` · then: `A WORD THAT DOESN'T LET IT SLIDE.`

If you don't know it, rest on three words, breathing in on light and out on from light. If you pray, the creed itself is a prayer you can say.

segments.voice: Yesterday, consubstantial: one in being, the Son begotten, not made. Your line was god from god.

"For Christ our pasch is sacrificed." That's Saint Paul, writing to the church in Corinth. The pasch is the Passover; Paul calls Christ the Passover lamb. So the feast of the resurrection grew up in the Passover season, a spring feast reckoned by the moon. And reckoning by the moon is harder than it sounds. Which full moon? Which Sunday after it? The historian Eusebius records that, well before Nicaea, churches in different places had answered those questions differently. Today, the other question the bishops carried to Nicaea: the date of Easter.
screen: `CHRIST OUR PASCH.` → `A SPRING FEAST, RECKONED BY THE MOON.` → `WHICH SUNDAY?`

segments.voice: Who the Son is was the great question at Nicaea. But by the account Eusebius preserves, the council also took up something that sounds smaller: the day of Easter. Eusebius keeps a letter the emperor Constantine sent to the churches after the council, urging everyone to keep the feast on one and the same day, so the Church would not be split over the feast of the resurrection. A practical problem with a deep root: if one church is still fasting while the church down the road is singing alleluia, does it look like one Church? The hope at Nicaea was a single day. Over the centuries, though, East and West came to reckon the date by different calendars. Today Catholic and Orthodox Christians keep the same resurrection, in some years on the same Sunday, and in some years not. Notice what this disagreement is not. It isn't about whether Christ rose; both proclaim it. It's a quarrel about the calendar, which is part of why it aches: so small, and still unsettled. The Second Vatican Council said it would not object to fixing Easter on a set Sunday, provided the other churches agreed. The door is open; nobody has walked through it alone, because the whole point is to walk through together. One day, someday. This week ran from Kyiv's river and the two lungs, through the Fathers, to the councils: what a council is, Nicaea, one word for who the Son is, and today, one day for the feast.

If you pray, ask God for the day when the whole Church sings alleluia on the same morning; if you don't, just wish it for them.
